source_text: Certe hanc concupiscentiam, sine qua nulla fecunditas est, malam naturaliter definisti; unde ergo per donum caeleste in senibus excitatur? Adstrue iam hoc, si potes, ad opus diaboli pertinere, quod Deum vides conferre pro munere
pass_a_gloss: Certainly this desire, without which there is no fruitfulness, you have defined as evil by nature; whence then is it aroused in old people through a heavenly gift? Now establish this, if you can, as belonging to the devil's work, which you see God confer as a gift.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae

pass_b_english: You have certainly defined as evil by nature this desire without which there is no fruitfulness. How, then, is it aroused in old people through a heavenly gift? Now establish, if you can, that something you see God bestow as a gift belongs to the devil’s work.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Augustine's quoted claim that the unbaptized remain under the devil; keep the personal devil, not 'evil'.
rejected: under Satan (name not in the Latin here)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, De nuptiis et concupiscentia 2 / On Marriage and Concupiscence); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
